p: The aviation medical examiner in Englewood worked out of a second floor office above a dentist, and the whole waiting room smelled faintly of mint and drill.

Jordan had filled out the MedXPress form the way she filled out a patient care report, every box, nothing rounded off. The doctor read it with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, listened to her heart for longer than she thought he needed to, and asked how she was sleeping. She told him the truth. Four hours, five on a good night, since March. He wrote something down, asked two more questions, and then asked a third that wasn't on any form: was she planning to fly tired. She said no. He looked at her the way she looked at drunk drivers who said they'd only had two, and then he signed.
FAA medical certificate, third class. Name: JORDAN E. REYES. Class: THIRD. Limitations: NONE. This certificate shall be valid for the period prescribed in 14 CFR 61.23.

It was a piece of paper the size of an index card. She'd expected to feel something about it. Mostly she felt the same thing she'd felt in April, when the whole family had gone in for heart screening because that's what you do after a sudden cardiac arrest at 41. Echo, ECG, a cardiologist with cold hands who said "normal" like he was handing her a present. She'd driven home from that one and sat in the driveway for twenty minutes. This time she just put the card in her wallet behind her driver's license and went to get a burrito.
Her phone buzzed in the parking lot. Another number she didn't have saved. She was starting to think the airport had a phone tree.

A text from Marisol Tran. This is Marisol. I do the wrenching on Biscuit. Abby says you read the whole checklist. Saturday 8am, hangar six. Cowling's coming off for an oil change. Wear clothes you hate.

Jordan read it in the car. She knew the name. Danny had said it a few hundred times over the years, usually as a verdict. "Marisol says it's fine." "Marisol says absolutely not." At the funeral a woman with short gray streaked hair and a work jacket had stood at the very back, left before the reception, and sent flowers with a card that said only BISCUIT MISSES YOU TOO.
She texted back: I'll be there. Then, after a minute: I don't own clothes I hate. I'll wear work pants.
The reply came instantly. You'll hate them by noon.
Abby's Ground School: what's under the cowling.

Marisol's got the cowling off, so we're doing this in the hangar today. Watch your head on the wing, everybody hits it once, me included, twice. See the grease pencil drawing on her whiteboard? One cylinder, one piston, two valves, and an arrow that says SUCK SQUEEZE BANG BLOW. Honestly that's the whole engine. I'm not erasing it.

What you're looking at is a Lycoming O-320. Four cylinders lying flat, two a side, cooled by air, 160 horsepower on a good day, fed by a carburetor. Each cylinder does the same four things over and over. Intake, the suck: piston goes down, intake valve opens, fuel and air come in. Compression, the squeeze: valve shuts, piston comes back up. Power, the bang: plugs fire, the mixture burns, and the pressure shoves the piston down, which turns the crankshaft, which turns the prop. Exhaust, the blow: exhaust valve opens and the piston pushes the burned stuff out the pipe. Four cylinders, each on a different stroke, more than a thousand times a minute while you sit there drinking coffee.

Spark comes from those two boxes bolted on the back. Magnetos. Think of a magneto as a tiny generator with a permanent magnet in it, spun by the engine. It makes its own high voltage. It doesn't want anything from your battery or your alternator, ever. There are two plugs in every cylinder and each mag fires one of them, so lose a mag, or a plug, and you lose a little power. That's it. The key switch has five spots: OFF, R, L, BOTH, START.

On the runup you test each mag alone. BOTH to R, little RPM drop, back to BOTH, then the same thing with L. A small drop's normal and the POH says how much is allowed. Big drop or a rough engine, think fouled plug or a bad lead. No drop at all sounds great and isn't. It can mean that mag's not getting grounded when you switch it off, so it's live all the time. Oh, and Biscuit's tach reads fifty high. Doesn't matter here, you're reading a difference, so the lie cancels out.

Which is why every prop is a live prop. Master off, key sitting on the glare shield, who cares. If a P lead, that's the ground wire between the mag and the switch, is broken and somebody moves the blade, the engine can fire. Marisol knows a guy. Ask her about him sometime, she'll tell you.

How the exam asks it. Know the strokes in order. Know that magnetos are independent of the electrical system, so an electrical failure doesn't stop the engine. Know that no drop on a mag check is a problem too.
The carburetor, carb ice, and the mixture.

Get down here with me and look up under the engine. That's the carburetor, the float kind. Air rushes up through a skinny throat called the venturi, which drops the pressure, and fuel sprays in and evaporates, and between those two things the temperature in there can fall 60 or 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Got moisture in the air and the inside of that thing gets to freezing? Ice grows on the throttle valve and in the venturi. It chokes the fuel and air, you lose power, and if enough piles up the engine quits.

The PHAK puts it this way: most likely below about 70°F (21°C) with relative humidity over 80 percent, and still possible as warm as 100°F (38°C) with humidity down near 50 percent. Low power is where it gets you, like a long descent, throttle mostly shut and the engine cooling off. It can sit there and grow and you won't know until you push the throttle in and nothing much happens. People find that out on short final. Don't be people.

In a fixed pitch prop airplane like Biscuit, your first clue is the RPM sagging. Roughness may follow. Fix: full carb heat, that knob pulls warm air from around the exhaust into the carburetor. Warm air's less dense, so the RPM dips a little more when you pull it. With ice in there, the engine may run rougher for a while as the melt goes through, then the RPM comes back up. No ice, RPM drops and just sits. The worst moment is the moment it gets worse, and that's exactly when people shove it back in. Leave it on. All the way. Partial heat can make it worse. Carb heat also costs you power, up to 15 percent, so it's off for takeoff.

The mixture's the red knob. It sets how much fuel goes with the air, and the carburetor's calibrated at sea level, which we are very much not. Climb, the air thins, the fuel doesn't, the mixture gets richer. Too rich wastes gas, runs rough, and cakes your plugs with carbon. Centennial is 5,885 feet, so you start out high just sitting on the ramp. We lean Biscuit for taxi, and Cessna's procedure at a high field is to lean for max RPM during a full throttle runup before takeoff. Coming down, you push it back in, because too lean runs hot and invites detonation. That's the mixture going off like a firecracker instead of burning, and it can wreck an engine. Lower grade fuel than the airplane wants, high power with the mixture way lean, and overheating all push you that direction.

How the exam asks it. Classic questions: the conditions for carb ice, the first indication (RPM loss with a fixed pitch prop), what RPM does when you apply carb heat with ice present (drops, then rises), and what happens to the mixture in a climb (it gets richer).

Biscuit's a high wing, so the fuel just runs downhill out of the wings into the carburetor. Gravity. There's no fuel pump to fail. That red handle on the floor, the famous sticky one, has LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH, and OFF, and the checklist wants BOTH for takeoff and landing. Every gallon that leaves a tank gets replaced by air coming in through the vents, so plug a vent and you can starve the engine while the wing's still half full. Every flight, you sample each tank drain and the strainer. Water, dirt, and color. Blue is 100LL. Anything else, you go find Marisol.

Oil keeps it cool and keeps it slippery. Oil pressure tells you right now when something's wrong. Oil temperature tells you slowly, like a friend who doesn't want to bring it up. High temp plus low pressure, together, you land.

Electricity runs the radios, lights, flaps, starter, fuel gauges, and the turn coordinator. Once the engine's running, an alternator bolted to it charges the battery and carries the load. Your master's split, BAT on one half and ALT on the other. The ammeter says whether the alternator's keeping up. Needle on the minus side, you're spending battery faster than you're putting it back. A steady discharge, the needle sitting left of center and staying there, usually means the alternator isn't carrying the load anymore. Full scale plus points at the voltage regulator. Either way, open the POH, turn off everything you don't need, and plan on landing, because now the battery is a clock.
Lose every bit of electrical power and guess what, the engine keeps running. Magnetos. You lose the radios, the lights, the electric flaps, and the fuel gauges turn into decorations.
How the exam asks it. Expect a center zero ammeter question. A steady discharge is the alternator, full scale plus is the regulator. And know that an electrical failure doesn't stop a magneto engine.
Pitot static instruments and the gyros.

Six gauges on the panel. Three run on air pressure. Airspeed compares ram air from the pitot tube, the little tube sticking out under the left wing, against static pressure from the static port, that tiny hole on the side of the fuselage you'd never notice. The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator use static only.

Pitot blocked but the drain hole's open, airspeed drops to zero. Opening and drain both blocked, the airspeed indicator turns into a bad altimeter: higher as you climb, lower as you descend. Static port blocked, the altimeter freezes wherever it happened, the VSI flatlines at zero, and airspeed lies, reading low when you climb above that altitude and high when you go below it. Some airplanes have an alternate static source inside the cabin. Cabin air's at slightly lower pressure than outside, so on alternate static the altimeter reads a bit high, the airspeed a bit fast, and the VSI jumps up for a second. No alternate static? Break the glass on the VSI. Cabin air gets into the system. You lose the VSI, which, fine.

The other three are gyros. In Biscuit the attitude indicator and the heading indicator spin on air sucked through them by an engine driven vacuum pump, and the suction gauge tells you that's happening. The turn coordinator's electric, on purpose, so a single failure doesn't take out all three. Gyros have rigidity in space, which the attitude and heading indicators lean on, and they precess when you push on them, which is how the turn coordinator works. Friction makes the heading indicator wander, so you reset it to the compass about every 15 minutes, straight and level, not accelerating.

Attitude indicator slowly leaning over like it's tired, heading indicator won't sit still? Look at the suction gauge. Low means the vacuum system is quitting on you. Turn coordinator, airspeed, and altimeter all still work. Fly those.

How the exam asks it. Blocked static: frozen altimeter, zero VSI. Blocked pitot with blocked drain: airspeed acts like an altimeter. Alternate static: everything reads a little high. Vacuum drives the attitude and heading indicators in most trainers.
Airworthiness: the paperwork that makes the airplane legal.

Now the boring part that grounds airplanes. Before you fly, certain documents have to be aboard, and the memory aid is AROW. A: the airworthiness certificate, displayed where passengers or crew can read it. That's 91.203. R: the registration certificate, also 91.203, and it now expires seven years after the last day of the month it was issued, per 47.40. O: operating limitations, meaning the approved flight manual or POH, the placards, and the instrument markings, under 91.9. W: the weight and balance data for this exact airplane. Older books say ARROW. The extra R was the FCC radio station license, and now you only need that if you're flying to another country.

Then the inspections. Those live in the maintenance logbooks, not in the airplane. The annual has to be done within the preceding 12 calendar months, 91.409(a). Calendar months means you go to the end of the month: an annual signed on August 14 is good through August 31 the next year. Only an A&P with an inspection authorization, or certain repair stations, or the manufacturer, can do an annual. Marisol has her IA, which is why she gets to sign Biscuit's.

The 100 hour inspection, 91.409(b), applies when the airplane carries anyone for hire who isn't crew, or when someone gives flight instruction for hire in an airplane that person provides. Read that last part twice. You can go over the 100 hours by up to 10, but only to fly to a place where the inspection can be done, and the extra time comes out of the next interval. An annual counts as a 100 hour. A 100 hour doesn't count as an annual.

The ELT runs on two clocks, both in 91.207. It has to be inspected within 12 calendar months of the last inspection. Its battery has to be replaced when the transmitter's been used for more than one cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life has expired, and the new expiration date gets marked on the outside of the transmitter and written in the records. The transponder needs a test every 24 calendar months before you can use it, 91.413, and here at Centennial, under the Denver Class B and its Mode C veil, you need it. You need ADS-B Out there too, 91.225, in the Mode C veil and under the Class B. The altimeter and static system test, every 24 calendar months, is required to fly IFR in controlled airspace, 91.411. For an airplane that only flies VFR it isn't legally required, though almost every owner gets it done with the transponder check. Airworthiness directives are mandatory, and the records have to show the status of each one, 91.417.

The owner or operator is responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy and the records straight. You're an owner now, so that's partly you. And as pilot in command, you confirm it before the wheels move.

How the exam asks it. Annual: 12 calendar months. 100 hour: only for hire, and the 10 hour overfly counts against the next one. ELT: 12 calendar month inspection, battery at 1 cumulative hour or half its useful life. Transponder: 24 calendar months. Altimeter and static system: 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace.
Required equipment, and flying with something broken.

For day VFR, 91.205(b) lists what has to be installed and working. Pilots remember it as TOMATO FLAMES: tachometer, oil pressure gauge, manifold pressure gauge (for an altitude engine), altimeter, temperature gauge (for a liquid cooled engine), oil temperature gauge (for an air cooled engine), fuel gauge for each tank, landing gear position indicator (for retractable gear), airspeed indicator, anticollision lights (only for small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996), magnetic compass, ELT (the mnemonic keeps it, but the requirement comes from 91.207, not 91.205), and seat belts and shoulder harnesses. Night adds FLAPS: fuses (a spare set, or three of each kind, that you can reach in flight), a landing light (only if you're operating for hire), anticollision lights (every airplane, at night), position lights, and a source of electrical power for everything installed.

When something's broken and the airplane has no MEL, and Biscuit doesn't, 91.213(d) is your process. First question: is it required? Check four places. The VFR day type certification requirements. The airplane's equipment list, or its Kinds of Operations Equipment List. 91.205 or any other rule for this flight. And any airworthiness directive. If any of those requires it, you're not going. If none of them do, the item gets removed, or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE, and any maintenance that takes gets logged under Part 43. Then a certificated pilot or a qualified mechanic decides it isn't a hazard. If it can't be deferred and can't be fixed where you are, a special flight permit can get the airplane to a shop.
Legal to defer doesn't mean smart to defer. One broken thing is a placard. Three broken things is a pattern.
And four broken things is a phone call to me, from under the wing. She's right about that too.

How the exam asks it. The test asks which items are required for day VFR, and what the steps are to fly with something inoperative without an MEL: not required, deactivated or removed, placarded INOPERATIVE, and determined not to be a hazard.
Decision one. Treat it like it's live.

Hangar Six was the sixth door in a long row of corrugated steel hangars on the north side of the field, and inside it Biscuit sat with her nose naked. The cowling lay on a moving blanket like a shell somebody had cracked open. Under it the engine was smaller than Jordan expected, four fat finned cylinders laid flat, two on each side, wires and tubes everywhere like the inside of a ten year old's model kit.

Marisol was on a rolling stool with a drain pan and did not get up. She was shorter than Jordan, with forearms like rope and a pencil behind each ear. A radio on the workbench was playing classic rock, volume at about two. On the back wall of the hangar was a whiteboard, half covered in block capitals Jordan knew from a lifetime of birthday cards. DUE LIST. ANNUAL 8/26. XPDR 10/26. ELT BATT 3/26. It hadn't been touched in a while. There was a calendar next to it from a parts supplier, still on March. A coffee can of spare fuel caps sat on the shelf under the board.
You're Jordan. Not a question. Okay. Lesson one. Go turn the prop for me, slowly, so you can feel the compression in each cylinder. She went back to the oil filter.
A. Turn it right away. The master's off and the battery is unplugged for the oil change.
B. Check that the key is out of the ignition and lying on the seat, then turn it.
C. Ask whether the mags are off and grounded, and still stay clear of the prop arc.
D. Grab a blade with both hands and swing it hard, so she can feel the strokes better.

Marisol stops wiping her hands on the rag. Mags off. Key's up on the glare shield. I checked both P leads before you got here, and I'll still yell if you put an arm through that arc. A pause. Who taught you that? YouTube. Also a guy on B shift named Hector, who has nine fingers and tells everybody why. Marisol almost smiles. Jordan stands off to the side and walks the blade around a few inches at a time, and each cylinder pushes back against her palm, slow and stubborn, four times per turn.
That's it. Right. Magnetos don't need the battery, so a broken P lead means a hot mag even with the key out. Confirm it's grounded, then still handle the prop like it's live. Both, every time.

Marisol pulled the air box off the bottom of the engine and handed Jordan the carburetor's guts to look at, more or less. A throat, a float bowl, a butterfly valve on a shaft. Air comes up through here and speeds up, pressure drops, fuel sprays in and evaporates. Same thing as an aerosol can getting cold in your hand. It can drop the temperature in there forty, fifty, sixty degrees.

She tapped the butterfly valve with a screwdriver. Ice grows right here. Your brother found that out the hard way, once. Ask him about it. She heard what she'd said a second after she said it. The screwdriver stopped moving. Then she cleared her throat. So. Quiz. Which day do you worry about this most?
A. Only when it's below freezing outside and there's already ice building on the wings.
B. A muggy 90°F afternoon, cruising at normal power with the windows cracked open.
C. A clear, dry January morning at 15°F, when everything is frozen solid already.
D. A cool, damp 60°F morning after rain, coming down at low power for a while.

Marisol points the screwdriver at her. That one. Every pilot thinks ice means winter. It's sixty degrees and wet, throttle mostly closed, engine cooling off. That's when it grows and you don't notice till you push the throttle in and nothing happens.

Yep. That's the one. Under 70 degrees, humidity high, low power in a descent. That's the bull's eye on the PHAK chart, and it's sneaky because nothing feels cold. Carb heat on before you pull the power back.

Marisol had all eight spark plugs out in a tray with numbered holes, a habit, she said, from a guy who once put them back in the wrong cylinders and spent an afternoon learning humility. She held one up to the light. The business end was crusted black and dry, like a match somebody blew out.
This one's from the bottom of number three. Tell me why it looks like that.
Jordan thought about the discovery flight. Abby taxiing out, the long wait behind a Cirrus at the runup area, the mixture knob all the way in the whole time because nobody told her to touch it.
A. Mixture too lean. The engine ran hot and burned the plug black.
B. Bad fuel. Someone put a lower grade in the tanks than Biscuit is rated for.
C. The plug is old and worn out. Replace it and the problem goes away.
D. Running full rich on the ground up here. At 5,885 feet that's too much fuel.

Yep. Carburetor thinks it's at sea level. It isn't. Lean it for taxi, lean it for the runup, and do what the POH says before takeoff up here. She drops the plug in the cleaner. Danny never leaned for taxi. I'd find these every oil change and yell at him, and he'd bring me a coffee, and we'd do it again.
Exactly right. Thinner air, same fuel, richer mixture. Rich runs cooler, doesn't burn completely, and leaves carbon on the plugs. At a high field you lean on the ground and enrich as you descend.
Marisol sent her to walk the airplane while the oil drained. Everything you looked at Saturday with Abby, look at again. I'll know if you didn't.

Under the left wing, behind the strut, the little bent fuel vent tube hung down like a soda straw. Jordan crouched to look up into it. It was packed with something gray and papery. When she tapped it, a wasp walked out, looked at her, and flew away unbothered.
A. Show Marisol, and treat Biscuit as grounded until the vent is cleared and checked.
B. Fly it. If fuel stopped flowing, the fuel gauges would show it right away.
C. Leave it. The fuel caps have their own vents, so this one doesn't matter.
D. Poke the nest out with a bit of safety wire herself, then go on with the walkaround.

Marisol crouches beside her, looks up the tube, and swears quietly in two languages. She clears it with a wire and blows air through until Jordan, standing at the fuel cap, can hear it whistle. That's the third one this spring. They love this airplane. She writes it on a squawk sheet. Then she writes the date.

That's it. Blocked vent, no fuel flow, quiet engine, usually right when you least want it. Show the mechanic, clear it properly, prove air moves through it. Then write it down so the next person knows to look.
Decision five. The battery is a clock.

By ten thirty the new oil was in and Marisol was safety wiring the oil filter. She finished it, looked at it for a while, snipped it off with a pair of dikes, and started over. The first one had looked perfect to Jordan, a tight little braid. She kept that to herself. Out on the ramp a fuel truck backed up with that beeping that never stops. Somebody out there was trying to start a Cherokee and it wasn't going well.

Next quiz, since you're just standing there. Night flight, you're over Limon on the way home, and the ammeter needle slides left of center and sits there, a steady discharge. What's happening, and what do you do?
She didn't look up from the wire. Jordan was getting the idea that this was what Marisol sounded like when she liked you.
A. The alternator has quit. Shut off what she doesn't need and plan to land soon.
B. Turn the whole master off to save the battery, and fly home in the dark.
C. Ignore it for now. The battery is probably just charging after the engine start.
D. The engine is about to quit, so pick a field and set up for a landing right now.

Yep. Engine doesn't care, the mags have it. Radios and lights care a lot. Landing light off, second radio off, call Denver while you can still talk to them, and go find a runway before that battery's dead.

Yep. That's the one. A steady discharge means the alternator isn't carrying the load. The engine runs fine on the magnetos, but the battery is now a clock. Shed the load, check the POH, talk to ATC early, land at the nearest suitable airport.
Decision six. Tape on the port.

Marisol had washed Biscuit on Friday, which explained why she was the cleanest thing in the hangar. On her second lap around the airplane, Jordan found a square of blue painter's tape stuck neatly over the static port on the side of the fuselage, a little hole she'd only learned the name of a week ago.
Good. I tape it when I wash. Takes it off before anybody flies. She said it with complete confidence. Then she added, more quietly, Usually.
Say it stayed on. You take off. What do the instruments do?
A. Only the airspeed indicator would be wrong. The pitot tube under the wing handles altitude.
B. The altimeter would freeze, so she'd just use the GPS altitude to fly the pattern.
C. The altimeter freezes, the VSI sits at zero, and the airspeed reads wrong in the climb.
D. Nothing much. Biscuit's alternate static source would take over by itself.

That's it. Altimeter stuck at field elevation. VSI dead flat. Airspeed reading low as you climb, because the trapped pressure behind it is higher than outside. She peels the tape off and hands it to Jordan. Keep that. Stick it on your kneeboard. It's a good reminder.

Exactly right. Blocked static: the altimeter freezes where the blockage happened, the VSI reads zero, and airspeed is wrong. It reads low as you climb above that altitude and high as you descend below it.
At noon they ate gas station sandwiches on overturned buckets. Jordan asked where the maintenance logbooks were.

Marisol pointed her sandwich at a fireproof file box on the workbench. Airframe, engine, prop. Fifty years of other people's handwriting. Everything that matters is on the board. She meant Danny's whiteboard. Nobody reads those cover to cover. Owners never do.

At work, Jordan read every line of every run report she signed, including the ones she wrote, because the time you skim is the time a dose is wrong. She looked at the box. She looked at the board, which hadn't been touched since March.
A. Look up N4791E on the FAA registry website and check that everything is current.
B. Check the latest annual entry in the logbook, and trust the board for the rest.
C. Trust the whiteboard and Marisol. She's the mechanic, and keeping track is her job.
D. Read through the logbooks herself and build a due list from the entries.

Knock yourself out. Jordan opens a legal pad and starts with the most recent annual, then works backward, one line at a time: date, tach time, what was done, who signed. Marisol goes back to the airplane, then comes back to look over her shoulder twice, pretending to need a wrench from the bench.
That's it. Read the source. The logbooks are the record, and the board is just someone's copy of it. Build your own list and compare. That's how you find where the copy went stale.

It took her an hour and forty minutes. The annual: August 14 last year, signed by Marisol with her IA number. The transponder and static system checks: October two years ago, at the avionics shop on the south side. The ELT inspection: done with the annual. All of it matched the board.

Then a three year old entry for an ELT battery replacement, with a line at the end in Marisol's neat capitals: NEW BATTERY EXPIRATION 03/2026. Jordan got up, walked to the tail, and opened the access panel where Marisol had shown her the ELT that morning. The label on the side of the transmitter said the same thing. REPLACE BATTERY 03/2026.
It was May. Danny had died in March. Out in the hangar, Marisol was singing along to a classic rock station, badly, and fixing the fuel selector detent for the second time that day.
A. Post it in the partners' group chat so all four owners see it at once.
B. Show Marisol the logbook entry and the ELT label side by side, dates and all.
C. Say nothing. Marisol did the annual. She must already know about it.
D. Text Walt first, since he's the club safety officer and has to know.

Marisol reads the logbook line. Then the label. Then the logbook line again. She doesn't say anything for long enough that the song on the radio ends. Then she says, very calmly, I wrote that. I wrote it right there in my own handwriting, and I told him to put it on the board, and he did. She sets the logbook down too carefully. And then I stopped looking at the board, because he always looked at the board.
Yep. That's the one. Just the facts and the dates, to the person who owns the records, in person. No blame in it. You'd be amazed how fast that gets a problem fixed.
Decision nine. Can it fly Tuesday.

Marisol was on the phone with the parts counter at the shop across the field within two minutes. They'd have a battery Monday. She hung up and kicked the rolling stool across the hangar, not hard, and then went and got it and sat on it.
Russ flew it to Steamboat in April. Over the Divide. With a dead ELT battery, and I'm the one who should've caught it. She wasn't talking to Jordan, exactly.
Jordan had a lesson with Abby on Tuesday morning. Her shifts didn't move. She asked the only question she had.
A message from Russ Kim. wait. i flew it over the divide last month. with an expired elt battery. cool. cool cool cool. marisol i'm buying you a beer and also never flying again
A. Fly Tuesday as planned. The annual is current, so the airplane is airworthy.
B. Placard the ELT inoperative under 91.213(d), then fly wherever they want.
C. Wait for the new battery, with the new date marked on the ELT and in the logbook.
D. Fly Tuesday's lesson under 91.207's exception for local training within 50 NM.

Marisol nods once. Monday. I'll swap it, run the test, mark the new date on the case and in the book. You fly Tuesday. She stands up, walks to the whiteboard, and draws a box around ELT BATT 3/26 without erasing it.

Exactly right. 91.207(c): when half the battery's useful life is gone, it gets replaced, and the new expiration goes on the outside of the transmitter and in the maintenance record. One day of waiting and the airplane is right everywhere it goes.
Decision ten. Who provides the airplane.

Walt came by at three, as promised, for the first of his monthly logbook checks. He read Jordan's pilot logbook, all 0.9 hours of it, with his glasses on the end of his nose, initialed the bottom of the page, and then listened to Marisol tell him about the ELT battery without interrupting once.
When she finished he said, That's on all four of us. Then he picked up Jordan's legal pad and read her due list. At the bottom she'd written: 100 HR, DUE TACH 2,441.8? WHY? She'd circled WHY twice.
Go ahead, he said. Tell me why you think Biscuit gets a 100 hour.
A. It's never needed. The annual covers everything, so the club can skip it.
B. It's not required by law here, but the club agreement requires one anyway.
C. Any airplane with more than one owner needs one, because the costs are shared.
D. It's required by law because Abby is being paid to give her instruction.

Walt takes his glasses off. Correct. Abby's paid, but she isn't providing the airplane. You are, as an owner. So the law says annual only. I wrote the 100 hour into the agreement in 2009, because four people fly this thing and Abby teaches in it, and I don't like finding out about things at the annual. He hands the pad back. Good question to circle.

That's it. 91.409(b) covers carrying people for hire, and flight instruction for hire in an airplane the instructor provides. Jordan's a co-owner paying an independent CFI, so it doesn't apply by law. The club's agreement does, so the club tracks it like it does.

Tuesday came in gray and damp. It had rained overnight and the ramp was still dark with it, puddles in the tie down rings, the windsock limp. Biscuit had a new ELT battery, a new date in marker on the transmitter, a new line in the logbook in Marisol's capitals, and a fresh box drawn on the whiteboard.
A text from Abby Strand. 10 min out. Tower closes the north runway at 9 for paint, so we're on a clock. Be ready to start when I get there.
Jordan had the checklist in her hand. Marisol had been through every inch of this engine on Saturday. The oil was brand new. The cowling had been off and on and signed for.
A. Do the full walkaround, but trust Saturday's oil entry instead of pulling the dipstick.
B. Run the whole checklist, everything Marisol touched included, even if Abby waits.
C. Run the checklist from memory to save time. She's done it three times now.
D. Skip the items Marisol worked on Saturday. She's an A&P, and she signed for them.

Oil on the dipstick, the cap tight. Every cowling fastener. Static port clear, no tape. Fuel vent clear. Three cups of fuel, blue all the way down. It takes twenty two minutes and Abby waits for six of them, drinking coffee and saying nothing. Find anything? No. Good. That's what a preflight usually finds. You do it for the time it doesn't.

Yep. That's the one. The preflight is the pilot's check, every flight, no matter who touched the airplane last. A clock is a reason to start early, never a reason to skip. If the lesson runs short because the preflight ran long, fine.

They took off on 35R and the door popped at rotation, like always. Jordan reached up and latched the top before Abby could open her mouth, and Abby snorted into the intercom. Out east the plains had gone green overnight, the air smooth and heavy as soup. The ATIS said thirteen degrees Celsius, dewpoint ten. She'd written that on her kneeboard right next to the strip of blue tape.

Abby had her fly a long slow descent at low power, 7,500 down to 6,500, then level off. Jordan pushed the throttle in. The RPM came up about halfway and quit coming. Then Biscuit started to shake, an ugly lopsided shudder through the floor and up into the yoke, a washing machine with one wet towel in it.
For one bad second all she could think about was the phone call from Claire in March.
Abby didn't touch anything. Your airplane. Talk to me.
A. Pull full carb heat, leave it on, and keep flying while it runs rougher for a bit.
B. Move the fuel selector to LEFT, in case it's a fuel problem from one tank.
C. Pull carb heat for a few seconds, and push it back in when the shaking gets worse.
D. Lean the mixture until the roughness smooths out, then fly home to Centennial.

She pulls the knob all the way out. The RPM sags another hundred and the shaking gets worse, much worse, for maybe twenty seconds that feel like a week, and she keeps her hand off the knob and holds altitude because that's the only job she has. Then it smooths out, all at once, like somebody flipped a breaker, and the tach needle climbs. She breathes out. Carb ice, Abby says. In May. At thirteen degrees. Now you'll never forget it.

Exactly right. Fixed pitch prop, RPM loss, then roughness, on a humid day after low power. Full carb heat, all the way, and leave it. It gets worse as the ice melts and then it gets better. Next time, carb heat on before you pull the power back.

Abby wrote up the lesson in the briefing room, 1.4 dual, and in the remarks put CARB ICE RECOGNITION AND RECOVERY, which made it sound much calmer than it had been. Jordan said she'd be a minute and walked back out to Biscuit.

She sat in the left seat with the door open and took the green composition notebook out of her bag. She'd been reading it a few entries at a time, rationing it. She flipped forward to see if he'd ever written about this. He had.

Danny's logbook, a page from June, seven years ago. June 3. KAPA local, 1.2. Pretty morning, 64 and wet after a storm. Long descent to Front Range, throttle back, admiring the view like a tourist. Added power, engine ran like a blender full of gravel. Pulled carb heat. It got WORSE. Which the book says it does. Which I forgot for the three longest seconds of my life. Then smooth as butter. Ice. In June. In Colorado. Carb heat on before every power reduction from now on. Marisol says she told me so. Marisol has told me so about everything.

Jordan laughed out loud, alone in the airplane, and then had to sit for a second with her hand over her mouth. Same airplane, same descent, same blender. He'd been scared exactly the way she'd been scared, and he'd written it down so somebody would know.

Back in the hangar Marisol was on the stepladder at the whiteboard. Under Danny's block capitals she was writing a new list in her own small neat ones, every item Jordan had found in the logbooks, with dates and tach times. She hadn't erased a single letter of his. The ELT line had a box around it and a new date beside it.
You find anything else in there, you tell me first, she said without turning around. Before Walt. Before the chat. Before Russ, God help us.

Marisol climbed down, opened the lid of her big red toolbox, and stood looking into it for a while. Jordan could see the inside of the lid from where she was. Taped to it, between a torque chart and a faded photo of a Super Cub on skis, was a short piece of safety wire twisted into an ugly lumpy spiral. Under it, on masking tape, in Marisol's capitals: D. REYES 2017. DO NOT FLY.

My divorce was 2017, Marisol said. Bad one. I was in here every weekend because I didn't want to be at the house. And your brother started showing up Saturday mornings with two coffees, saying he wanted to learn to safety wire. Every Saturday for a year. He was terrible at it. Worst hands I ever saw on a grown man. He never got any better, and he never stopped coming. She touched the wire with one finger. Took me till about Christmas to figure out he wasn't there to learn anything.

Jordan hadn't known. Nobody in the family had known. Danny had told them about Moab and dirt strips and the time he saw a bald eagle off the wingtip. He'd never once mentioned a year of Saturdays sitting on a bucket in a hangar, being bad at something on purpose so a friend wouldn't be alone.

He made that board so I wouldn't have to keep the list in my head anymore, Marisol said. And I let him. And then he was gone and the list just stopped. She closed the toolbox lid gently. Something soft shifted inside, a padded bag of some kind, and she put her hand flat on the lid as if to keep it there. You don't read like him, you know. He never read anything. You read like somebody who'd have caught it.
Jordan drove home with the strip of blue tape still stuck to her kneeboard. On the seat beside her the phone buzzed once.
A text from Abby Strand. Thursday 7am if the weather plays nice. Check the TAF before you text me. If you don't know what a TAF is, that's next week.
